extracted.intended_audience: citizens, delegates, and policymakers considering the structure and powers of a national constitution (readers of The Federalist / informed public)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for structuring an effective national government (distribution of powers, revenue, military, judiciary, representation, and legitimacy) to preserve union, security, and justice. Focused on constitutional design choices and their practical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction to federal laws (enforceability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States, as now composed, have no powers to exact obedience, or punish disobedience to their resolutions, either by pecuniary mulcts, by a suspension or divestiture of privileges, or by any other constitutional mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A national government must have an express constitutional sanction—authority to enforce its laws against delinquent members. Without such delegated enforcement power, the Union exhibits a government 'destitute even of the shadow of constitutional power to enforce the execution of its own laws.' The text contrasts this defect with other confederacies and frames it as a primary cause of national impotence and instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual guaranty of State governments
rubrics_metrics.description: The want of a mutual guaranty of the State governments is another capital imperfection in the federal plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A federal guaranty should protect states from domestic usurpation and violent overthrow of their constitutions. The guaranty is not intended to impede lawful, peaceable reforms by a state's people; it operates against changes effected by violence. Without it, successful factions or usurpers could erect tyranny in one state that would threaten the whole Union (e.g., the dangers manifested in Massachusetts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal authority to raise its own revenues
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no method of steering clear of [inequality from quotas], but by authorizing the national government to raise its own revenues in its own way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The national government should be empowered to levy imposts, excises, and duties on consumption (indirect taxes) rather than depend on state requisitions. This allows the federal treasury to supply national exigencies without relying on unequal state assessments. Direct authority to raise revenue prevents the inequities and enforcement problems of requisitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject quotas/requisitions for state contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of regulating the contributions of the States to the common treasury by QUOTAS is another fundamental error in the Confederation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotas (apportioning contributions by measures like land value or population) are impractical and unjust because there is no common standard of national wealth. Such rules produce glaring inequality and oppression, aggravate resentment among states, and may ultimately destroy the Union if enforcement were possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer indirect taxes (imposts/excises) as self-limiting revenue source
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposts, excises, and, in general, all duties upon articles of consumption ... contain in their own nature a security against excess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect taxes (duties on consumption) are naturally self-limiting: excessively high duties reduce consumption and thus revenue. They typically constitute the chief part of national revenue, and their 'fluid' nature helps distribute burdens in relation to citizens' resources. If particular duties create inequalities between states, those may be counterbalanced by other duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of direct taxes (apportionment and practicality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those of the direct kind, which principally relate to land and buildings, may admit of a rule of apportionment. Either the value of land, or the number of the people, may serve as a standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct taxes (on land/buildings) can be apportioned and, for simplicity and certainty, population (numbers) is preferred as a practical standard. Accurate land valuation is difficult and expensive, especially in a developing country, so fixed rules may mitigate the arbitrary discretion of government in direct taxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal power to regulate commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: The want of a power to regulate commerce is by all parties allowed to be of the number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A national commerce power is essential to secure consistent foreign treaties, prevent clashing state regulations, and avoid interstate jealousies and retaliatory regulations. Without federal superintendence, separate state prohibitions and restrictions frustrate beneficial treaties and give foreign powers opportunities to exploit divisions (examples: failed coordinated measures; analogy to German multiplicity of duties).

rubrics_metrics.name: National authority over raising and governing armed forces
rubrics_metrics.description: The authorities essential to the common defense are these: to raise armies; to build and equip fleets; to prescribe rules for the government of both; to direct their operations; to provide for their support. These powers ought to exist without limitation ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defense powers must be broad (not shackled) because national exigencies are unforeseeable. Relying on state quotas for men caused auction-like competition for bounties, short enlistments, undisciplined forces, slow levies, and unequal burdens (states near danger furnished more men). A centralized power avoids inefficiency and inequality in military mobilization and support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against equal suffrage of states (favor proportional representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of equal suffrage among the States is another exceptionable part of the Confederation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giving equal votes to states of vastly unequal population violates principles of fair representation and majority rule: a majority of states might be a minority of the people. Equal suffrage risks larger states revolting at being governed by disproportionately small states and contravenes republican norms that the sense of the majority should prevail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unanimity/high supermajority requirements (prevent paralysis and corruption vulnerability)
rubrics_metrics.description: To give a minority a negative upon the majority ... is, in its tendency, to subject the sense of the greater number to that of the lesser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring large consensuses (or unanimity) obstructs government action, causes delays, and substitutes the caprice or artifices of a small minority for the decisions of a respectable majority. It also increases susceptibility to foreign bribery and corruption (harder to corrupt a greater number than a small one), illustrated by examples like the Polish diet and potential wartime treaty-making impediments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a national judiciary (one supreme tribunal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A circumstance which crowns the defects of the Confederation remains yet to be mentioned, the want of a judiciary power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws and treaties require courts to expound their meaning; without a supreme tribunal there will be divergent final determinations among state courts. A national supreme court, instituted under the same authority as treaties, is necessary to produce uniformity, avoid contradictory judgments, prevent local bias, and ensure treaties and national laws have consistent operation across the Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation of the constitution on the consent of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: It has not a little contributed to the infirmities of the existing federal system, that it never had a ratification by the PEOPLE ... The fabric of American empire ought to rest on the solid basis of THE CONSENT OF THE PEOPLE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratification by state legislatures alone leaves the federal compact vulnerable to claims of repeal by those legislatures. Popular ratification secures deeper legitimacy and prevents instability arising from unilateral state actions to revoke national compacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate distribution and organization of governing institutions (avoid concentrating expanded powers in a single assembly)
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization of Congress is itself utterly improper for the exercise of those powers which are necessary to be deposited in the Union. A single assembly may be a proper receptacle of those slender, or rather fettered, authorities ... but it would be inconsistent with all the principles of good government, to intrust it with those additional powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When substantially greater powers are to be vested in the national government, institutional organization must change accordingly (checks, separation, multiple bodies). Concentrating expanded prerogatives in one body risks either the machine's decay or the accumulation of all sovereign prerogatives in a single assembly, potentially producing tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect national faith and foreign confidence by preventing state-level subversion of treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: The treaties of the United States, under the present Constitution, are liable to the infractions of thirteen different legislatures, and as many different courts of final jurisdiction ... The faith, the reputation, the peace of the whole Union, are thus continually at the mercy of the prejudices, the passions, and the interests of every member ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaties and national engagements must be backed by unified national mechanisms (law and judiciary) so that foreign nations can rely on consistent performance. Disparate state-level control over treaties undermines international respect and the security of national commitments.
